text: Every course so far handed you a tool. This one hands you a problem. Over the next twenty-three lessons you'll take one messy business dataset from a vague request to a deployed model, a stakeholder presentation, and a portfolio project you can show an employer. Lessons one through fifteen are the project itself; sixteen through twenty-three turn it into a resume, a GitHub portfolio, and interview prep.

You've been hired as the data scientist at Harvest Table, a fictional meal-kit subscription company. Customers pay weekly for boxes, choose a Basic, Family, or Premium plan, and can cancel anytime. The head of retention asks you for a list of currently active customers most likely to cancel in the next sixty days, how much to trust that list, and how it fits into their systems. That's the whole assignment — no target column, no feature list, no metric. Turning it into those things is lessons two and three.

The workflow follows the order of the whole path: business problem, SQL, Python, exploratory analysis, model, evaluation, deployment, presentation. Nothing here re-teaches SQL, pandas, scikit-learn, or MLOps — you already have every skill. These lessons show how the pieces fit together on a project where the data is imperfect and the answer isn't in the back of the book.

The data is entirely synthetic, generated from a fixed seed with numpy and pandas, so everyone who runs make_data.py gets the identical database: harvest_table.db, with customers, orders, tickets, and cancellations tables. The script deliberately plants messiness you'll need to find and fix.

A quick SQL audit turns up exactly what was planted: forty duplicate customer rows, sixteen different spellings of four regions, a hundred fifty-nine missing ages plus twelve impossible ones, eight hundred fifty-five signup dates in the wrong format, and over fourteen hundred order amounts stored as dollar-sign strings. Write these down — lessons four and five fix each one with a documented rule. Next: turning the retention head's request into a precise prediction problem.
